title: R01 — Imaging an incompletely visualized persistent neck mass
fairness: Contrast-enhanced neck CT is the defensible best offered study for this incompletely mapped persistent adult neck lesion. MRI is not offered, so its potential appropriateness does not create a second key.
The task is complete and the presentation supplies age, sex, clinical stability and the relevant ultrasound limitation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The imaging task already presupposes further assessment. Persistence does not supply a separate consequential inference within these options: repeat the limited study, obtain local cross-sectional imaging, or undertake systemic metabolic imaging. This is a familiar modality-selection rule with weak competition, rather than two consequential steps.
R01's explanation does not disclose R02's sampling technique or target. The transition from ultrasound to the subsequent CT record is coherent.

Review-wide scope: all 12 proposed executable nodes were assessed using their candidate presentation/profile, current update, exhibit, task, option labels and explanation. Key position and author difficulty/acceptance claims were not evidence. The one kept legacy record, 11 proposed legacy retirements and separate unscored functioning-nerve invasion hold were noted but not independently adjudicated. No held or parked node was treated as executable.

Review-wide limitations: this is an offline editorial review, not independent source verification or clinical approval. All versions remain needs_clinician_review. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative educational judgments, not measured exam frequencies. Runtime rendering, answer randomization and wait estimates cannot be certified from the permitted visible fields; no fixed waits occur in this candidate prose. Each case supplies one consistent age/sex profile and a short complaint. All proposed exhibits are null.

No reliable wording-only shortcut uniquely separates CT from PET-CT; the concern is shallow clinical discrimination, not fabricated lexical cueing. Adult neck-mass evaluation is a high-yield objective.
suggestions: Retain the persistent lesion and actual acoustic limitation. Rebuild the decision around interpretation of a genuinely competing prior study or acquisition issue so a repeat examination remains initially reasonable and a specific observation changes the next study.
Replace the systemic-staging foil with a credible competing local workup strategy supported by the revised case. Do not merely add MRI and declare it inferior without a patient-specific reason.
If this remains a straightforward foundational imaging item, seek explicit acceptance of that role instead of describing it as difficult two-step resident reasoning.

title: R02 — Initial acquisition from a partly cystic neck mass

cues.phrase: Which initial tissue procedure / Ultrasound-guided FNA of the tissue component
cues.why: The task's tissue wording is repeated only in the key's target label. This is a weak lexical nudge, not proof that fluid sampling is never diagnostic; it reinforces an already elementary target contrast.

fairness: Image-guided FNA directed at viable enhancing tissue is the best offered initial acquisition. FNA of the fluid component is less representative; an initial open excision is a credible classic error but substantially less attractive at this stage. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Technique and target are nominally two choices, but one option is the familiar premature open-biopsy error and the remaining pair directly contrasts tissue with fluid. The actual discrimination is easy rather than two substantial reasoning steps.

The CT update coherently follows R01 and supplies accessible cervical tissue and lack of continuity with a major vessel. R01 feedback does not preteach this answer. With the shared presentation and this update, the question stands independently of answering R01 correctly.
The explanatory caveat about core sampling appropriately avoids a universal FNA-over-core claim. Adult cystic neck-mass sampling is high yield.
suggestions: Use a neutral complete lead-in such as which sampling procedure to request for the imaged cervical mass, avoiding key-only repetition of tissue.

Make technique and target selection depend on a clinically meaningful acquisition or adequacy finding and compare credible sampling plans at that same stage. Do not add core as a distractor without information that distinguishes it.
Retain the observed solid/fluid anatomy and vascular relationship; hiding those facts would impair fairness rather than improve difficulty.

title: R03 — Tissue architecture after unresolved lymphoid sampling
clarityIssues: The explanation's sentence about a new surgical-architecture objective and an old core-after-FNA rule refers to authoring history that a resident has not been given. It does not explain the clinical choice.

cues.phrase: Repeat core biopsy of a cervical node / Repeat FNA biopsy of a cervical node
cues.why: Both distractors explicitly repeat the two procedures that the presentation has just described as insufficient. The key is the only new acquisition, allowing a try-something-different strategy without understanding lymphoid architecture.

cues.phrase: He takes no anticoagulant and has no previous neck operation.
cues.why: Together with the superficial mobile node and vessel separation, these extra surgical-permission details point toward the sole operative option. The actual anatomy is relevant, but the cumulative scaffolding makes the intended escalation conspicuous.

fairness: Excisional biopsy is a defensible best answer for a suspected T-cell lymphoid process that remains unclassified after viable cores lacking preserved organization, when an accessible node is described. I do not identify a confident clinical error in the key.
The nodal-organization finding is decision-critical and should remain. It is legitimate pathology evidence, not an error merely because it supports excision.

The item mainly tests recognition that larger tissue architecture is needed after inadequate classification. The two already-unsuccessful repeat procedures do not sustain a second consequential decision. Lymphoma tissue architecture is high yield; exact subtype-specific acquisition claims still require clinician review.

This is a standalone node, with no sequence dependency. The ultrasound attribution of a mobile node is awkward: mobility is ordinarily a clinical examination observation, whereas the vessel relationship is an ultrasound finding.
suggestions: Replace authoring-history commentary with a short explanation of why viable cells can still fail to establish nodal architecture and why the offered repeat methods are less useful here.
Attribute mobility to examination and separation from vessels to ultrasound.

If retaining resident-level difficulty, make specimen adequacy or target selection genuinely distinguish a plausible repeat acquisition from excision; avoid making both distractors unqualified repeats of documented failures.
Trim nonessential procedural-permission details while preserving actual surgical accessibility and any real contraindication needed to rank the options.

title: N01 — Intervention after failed basket capture of a distal duct stone
fairness: Transoral incision and extraction is the defensible best offered intervention for a fixed distal submandibular duct stone reached but not captured endoscopically. The case does not imply that failed basket capture requires gland excision.

The two consequential steps are interpreting the failed procedure as a capture/impaction problem rather than failure to reach the stone, then using distal localization to select extraction over fragmentation or gland removal. These facts materially determine the action.

All three choices are specific procedures of comparable form. The anatomical words are necessary data, not a unique wording match to the key. No strong length, convergence, absolute or pre-answer teaching cue identified.

The clinical diagnosis is properly supplied for a treatment decision. Absence of fever or purulent drainage supports the nonacute treatment stage. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; comparisons with unoffered techniques are not needed to establish the best offered choice.

N01's explanation does not reveal N02's subsequent residual-stone management. The later stone-removal update follows coherently. Location-dependent management of symptomatic salivary stones is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve the exact distinction between reaching the stone and failing to pass a basket around it; do not simplify this to nonspecific failed sialendoscopy.
Keep this editorial PASS separate from Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical approval.

title: N02 — Asymptomatic residual intraparenchymal calcification
clarityIssues: The residual focus was not described in the initial presentation. The term still implies an earlier documented intraparenchymal focus, although the preceding record described only the distal duct stone. A resident can infer a second focus, but the chronology should state it directly.
fairness: Clinical follow-up is a defensible best answer for the asymptomatic residual intraparenchymal finding with restored clear salivary flow. The explanation says conservative follow-up can be appropriate and does not claim that all retained stones should always be ignored.

The symptom resolution is essential clinical evidence, not an unfair clue that should be removed. However, the offered alternatives are another extraction beyond the previously entered segment and removal of the now-functioning gland. This makes observation a straightforward choice with little remaining conflict.

The update is necessary and does change management from N01, but its interpretation and application amount to the single simple rule of not intervening merely to clear an asymptomatic image. The intraparenchymal detail mainly makes the procedural alternatives still less attractive.

The treatment response follows N01 coherently, and N01's explanation does not state this answer. Apart from the still chronology issue, the shared presentation plus update supports independent answering.

General symptom-driven salivary management is useful, but this exact residual intraparenchymal-stone surveillance distinction is lower-yield than initial neck-mass workup, symptomatic stone treatment or malignant facial-nerve findings. This is a qualitative prioritization, not a claim about measured exam frequency.
suggestions: Say follow-up ultrasound shows an additional intraparenchymal focus, or document that focus in the preceding record, without implying that the removed distal stone persists.
Consider merging this into N01's post-answer teaching instead of using another scored node for the uncomplicated recovery state.

If a separate resident-level node is retained, supply an evidence-supported residual symptom/function discrepancy that creates a real observation-versus-intervention decision. Do not manufacture pain or an unsupported stone-size threshold solely to raise difficulty.

title: N03 — Core versus repeat FNA for an indeterminate parotid sample
clarityIssues: The report cannot distinguish the candidate salivary tumor types does not identify what diagnostic distinction remains, whether malignancy was established, or why the obtained material cannot resolve it. Those omissions matter when comparing core with an optimized repeat FNA.

cues.why: The only repeat-labelled option immediately follows an unresolved FNA, while core is the new needle technique. This encourages a generic escalate-after-failure answer without establishing why repeat cytology would fail in this particular case.

fairness: Core biopsy is a plausible next acquisition. I cannot establish from these visible fields that it is uniquely preferable to a repeat FNA with improved cytopathology/ancillary support. Viable epithelial cells show that tissue was reached, but do not by themselves establish all relevant dimensions of cytologic adequacy or the reason histotype remains unresolved.

This is an uncertainty about the ranking, not a confident claim that core is incorrect. The explanation's supported next acquisition wording establishes acceptability rather than superiority over the closest distractor.

The superficial target and intact skin make an accessible percutaneous approach plausible; open incisional biopsy is a much weaker competitor. Two-step reasoning is not secure because the diagnostic limitation that should drive the second decision is unspecified.

The question is complete, and the subsequent core-established carcinoma in N04 is a coherent later result. N03's explanation does not leak N04's MRI answer. Salivary-mass sampling is high yield, but the uncertainty must not be counted as desirable difficulty.
suggestions: Specify the actual unresolved diagnostic distinction and the documented limitations of the reviewed FNA material, using clinician-supported findings rather than a generic cannot-distinguish statement.

Have clinical sign-off adjudicate whether those exact findings make core preferable to an optimized repeat FNA. If both remain defensible, change the competing plans or objective; do not declare a universal core-after-FNA ladder.
Make the explanation state the case-specific reason for choosing core over the closest alternative, rather than merely saying that core is supported.

title: N04 — Local imaging after parotid carcinoma and new nerve findings
clarityIssues: Sensation near the right ear has changed is vague: it gives neither the sensory alteration nor its distribution. If localization is intended to drive the imaging field, state the actual examination finding.

cues.phrase: best completes local assessment / FDG PET-CT of the body
cues.why: The lead-in asks for local assessment while one distractor explicitly offers a body study. Scope matching can discard it without interpreting the new findings.
This singles out the keyed modality as permissible. No competing constraint is being tested, so the sentence functions as unnecessary key-specific permission.

fairness: Contrast MRI of the neck and skull base is the defensible best offered local study with parotid carcinoma, new facial weakness and concern for neural/deep extension. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Bone-focused CT and body PET-CT address substantially different questions. Even without the new nerve findings, carcinoma with an unseen deep margin strongly favors the offered MRI over these alternatives. The symptom update therefore does not earn the claimed additional consequential inference.

The later carcinoma result and new weakness follow N03 coherently. The description should not imply weakness was documented as normal earlier when no baseline examination was supplied, but weaker at the next examination is understandable clinical chronology. N03 feedback does not disclose MRI.
The shared presentation and update make the node answerable without prior success. Malignant parotid nerve involvement is high yield; the current option set underuses that concept.
suggestions: Replace the vague sensory phrase with a specific supported examination observation if it is needed, otherwise remove it.
Remove the isolated MRI-permission sentence unless a genuine contraindication tradeoff is being tested.

Make the new neurological finding change a real local imaging or extent-assessment decision after an explicitly described prior study. Compare credible local requests with similar scope, and avoid making MRI the only option capable of addressing the stated task.
Reapply the update-deletion test: the deciding request should change or become genuinely unresolved when the new findings are removed.

title: N05 — Preservation of functioning separable facial nerve branches
clarityIssues: The explanation calls gross invasion a separate withheld boundary. Withheld is internal authoring language, not a clinical explanation for the resident.

cues.phrase: Preserve the exposed facial nerve branches / Resect the adjacent branches and graft them / Resect the main nerve trunk and graft it
cues.why: The key is the only preservation plan; both distractors resect an apparently functioning structure that the stem explicitly describes as separable and uninvolved. This contrast favors the key through ordinary preservation logic, before specialist operative reasoning.

cues.phrase: a plane opening between the tumor and facial nerve branches, with no tumor encasing or entering them
cues.why: These necessary observations nearly state the rationale for the sole preservation option. The defect is the absence of a credible competing decision, not that the operative observations should be hidden.

fairness: Preserving the functioning, grossly uninvolved, separable branches while resecting the tumor is the defensible best answer. Malignancy itself is not an indication to remove the facial nerve. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Normal preoperative movement and a free plane leave no substantial argument for either branch resection or main-trunk resection in this set. The node tests a high-yield preservation principle but not two consequential reasoning steps.

The retrospective operative task is explicit. The later small-nerve microscopic invasion in N06 does not contradict the gross operative observations or retroactively justify sacrificing the main facial nerve.
N05's feedback does not state N06's radiotherapy answer. The known carcinoma diagnosis is appropriate for this management question.
suggestions: Retain the functioning-nerve and gross-separation findings; removing them could create the disputed invaded-but-functioning-nerve scenario.

Either obtain explicit acceptance as a foundational preservation item or redesign around a different supported operative tradeoff that gives more than one credible initial plan. Do not cross into the held gross-invasion boundary to manufacture difficulty.
Replace withheld boundary with a brief clinical limitation explaining that management of actual gross neural invasion requires a different assessment.

title: N06 — Microscopic perineural invasion after complete low-grade tumor excision
fairness: Postoperative regional radiotherapy is the defensible best offered plan for multidisciplinary discussion when microscopic perineural invasion is found despite clear margins. Surveillance is a credible near-miss because the tumor is small, low grade and node negative. Routine cisplatin intensification is not established merely by this finding.

The learner must identify perineural invasion from tumor within small nerve sheaths, then apply that adverse feature despite otherwise favorable pathology. The update materially changes the surveillance-versus-adjuvant-treatment decision. These are two consequential steps.

The diagnosis label is withheld appropriately while the actual pathological observation is supplied. No unique wording echo, answer-length outlier, rhetorical absolute or pre-answer explanation identifies radiotherapy. The two radiotherapy-containing options still require deciding whether systemic intensification is warranted.

The small nerves are explicitly separate from the main facial nerve. This preserves coherence with N05 and makes the later question interpretable using the shared presentation and update. N05's explanation does not teach postoperative irradiation.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The recommendation is for team discussion, not a specified regimen or claim of guaranteed benefit. Exact histotype-specific evidence and final treatment planning remain for clinician review. Perineural invasion as an adverse postoperative feature is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve both the favorable pathology and the anatomically distinct microscopic nerve finding; those details create the useful competition with surveillance.
Keep the explanation's distinction between gross facial-nerve involvement and microscopic small-nerve invasion, and do not add an unsupported radiotherapy regimen or mandatory cisplatin rule.
Keep this editorial PASS separate from Melissa Rowland's exact-version clinical approval.

title: N07 — Imaging worsening parotid infection after a limited ultrasound
clarityIssues: The founder reviews a point before source control is awkward nonclinical framing. The question otherwise clearly identifies an outside inpatient timepoint rather than a current outpatient emergency.

cues.why: This reveals a later intervention before the learner interprets whether persistent symptoms and limited ultrasound suggest a drainable deep process. It supplies unnecessary hindsight.

cues.phrase: Repeat surface ultrasound of the parotid
cues.why: Surface echoes the stated failure to see the deep lobe and makes the repeat-study option advertise its limitation. The acquisition limitation belongs in the clinical record, not in a pejorative distractor label.

fairness: Contrast-enhanced neck CT is the defensible best offered study for worsening infection with trismus and an unvisualized deep lobe. A limited superficial ultrasound cannot establish absence of a deep collection, and noncontrast CT is less suited to defining an abscess and its extent.

There are two useful steps beneath the wording: distinguish an incompletely examined deep gland from a reassuring negative study, then select contrast cross-sectional assessment in a worsening course. This could be moderate resident reasoning after the hindsight and option-label cues are removed.

Handling secretions without stridor is relevant to the stated imaging decision. It does not prove airway safety in all circumstances, but the explanation appropriately preserves urgent airway assessment if deterioration occurs. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
This is a standalone retrospective node. Deep salivary infection, source assessment and recognition of inadequate imaging are high-yield principles.
suggestions: Replace the founder/source-control sentence with a direct neutral inpatient chronology, such as during the admission, fever persisted despite intravenous antibiotics and hydration.
Use a neutral repeat-ultrasound label while keeping the original acoustic limitation in the presentation.
Preserve the actual deterioration and airway observations. Reassess the clean version's difficulty; do not add unsupported antibiotic failure durations or arbitrary abscess thresholds.

title: N09 — Persistent fever and new chest pain after cervical drainage
clarityIssues: The founder reviews an outside hospital timepoint adds game-role framing to an otherwise clear retrospective clinical question. A direct hospital chronology would be easier to read.

cues.phrase: Contrast CT of the neck and chest / Contrast CT limited to the neck / CT pulmonary angiography of the chest
cues.why: The key combines the neck component of one distractor and the chest component of the other. It is also the only plan covering both symptom locations, while limited labels one alternative as incomplete. This creates a convergence/comprehensiveness shortcut without requiring recognition of descending infection.

fairness: Contrast CT covering the neck and chest is the defensible best offered investigation for persistent fever and new retrosternal pain after treatment of deep-neck infection. Improving visible neck swelling does not rule out inferior extension.

The intended two steps are meaningful: interpret discordant neck improvement and systemic/chest deterioration, then select an examination that maps the potentially connected compartments. Pulmonary angiography is a plausible competing chest-pain investigation but does not replace assessment of the cervical source.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The stable breathing and blood pressure support the proposed imaging stage without asserting that infection is benign.
The high-yield concept is recognition of descending mediastinal infection. The option construction makes this easier than its otherwise moderate clinical reasoning warrants.

N09's explanation names inferior extension and connected compartments. It does not name a drainage route, but it substantially scaffolds the anatomical interpretation tested by N10; N10 must be rated in that visible sequence.
suggestions: Retain improving neck findings alongside persistent fever and new retrosternal pain; that mismatch is the useful clinical discriminator.

Rebuild the alternatives as comparably complete diagnostic plans for plausible competing interpretations, rather than a neck-only/chest-only/both component matrix. Remove limited from the distractor label.
Use direct inpatient chronology instead of founder framing.
Ensure the follow-up asks a distinct consequential decision rather than merely relabelling the extension already explained here.

title: N10 — Source control for a separate mediastinal collection
clarityIssues: Below the thoracic inlet does not precisely define the inferior extent relevant to selecting a drainage approach. The explanation correctly defers exact access to specialist assessment; the answer should not be read as prescribing a particular transthoracic route from these data alone.

cues.phrase: It remains outside both pleural spaces. / Pleural catheter drainage of the right hemithorax
cues.why: The record explicitly excludes the compartment named in this distractor. No clinical inference is needed to discard it, and the unmotivated right-sided choice is especially weak.

cues.phrase: the original cervical cavity collapsed around its drain / Repeat drainage of the original cervical cavity
cues.why: The update describes successful collapse of the exact site named in the other distractor and calls the new pocket separate. A reader can reject the repeat-site option by direct text matching.

cues.phrase: behind the sternum, between the lungs, below the thoracic inlet
cues.why: Once the two explicitly excluded sites are removed, the learner only needs to match this anatomical description to the remaining mediastinal label. The raw wording has not created a consequential second decision.

fairness: Arranging specialist drainage/source control of the mediastinal collection is the defensible best offered plan while antibiotics continue. The stated findings do not support draining an uninvolved right pleural space or merely repeating drainage of the collapsed original cavity.

I do not identify a confident clinical error in this broad referral/source-control key. However, the extent given does not establish one operative access route; the explanation's qualification is necessary and should remain.

The task already asks for additional source control, and all answers are drainage procedures. The learner is therefore selecting a named compartment after both wrong compartments have been expressly excluded, not independently deciding whether/how a persistent infected focus changes treatment.

The follow-up is anatomically coherent with N09 and can be answered from the shared presentation and update alone. In the sequence it is even easier: N09's explanation has already identified inferior extension and connected neck/chest compartments.
Mediastinal infection requiring source control is high yield. The current node tests an elementary anatomical match rather than the important management reasoning.
suggestions: Preserve the observed separate pocket and its compartment; deleting the imaging findings to hide the key would impair clinical fairness.

Replace the two explicitly uninvolved-site distractors with credible management alternatives at the same decision stage. Supply verified extent, treatment response and other observations needed to distinguish them.

If testing drainage approach, provide the actual anatomical extent needed for that decision and obtain clinician adjudication of the competing routes. Do not infer a mandatory thoracic access route from below the inlet alone.

Alternatively merge this uncomplicated localization result into N09's feedback, or seek an explicit foundational-anatomy exception. Keep the later task distinct from the extension diagnosis already taught by N09.
